source: European Society of Radiology member survey (published 2022); FDA list of AI-enabled devices
comment: 276 of 690 responding ESR members (40%) had hands-on clinical experience with AI, above the 25% line. About three quarters of all AI-enabled devices authorised by the US regulator are for radiology. The survey reports experience, which is weaker than routine use, and respondents may be more interested in AI than the average radiologist. Found by web search; pages not opened by the assistant.

comment: A handheld AI-powered device for evaluating skin lesions was cleared in the US in January 2024. It uses light spectroscopy, not images, and is not cleared for screening. No named provider in routine use and no survey was found. Found by web search; page not opened.

comment: An AI algorithm that detects a weak heart pump function from a standard electrocardiogram was cleared in the US in 2023. Cardiovascular devices are the second largest group of authorised AI devices, at about a tenth of the list. No named provider in routine use and no survey was found. source: FDA clearance of smartwatch functions for detecting irregular heart rhythm, 2018
comment: Smartwatch functions that detect signs of atrial fibrillation have been cleared in the US since 2018 and are widely used by consumers. Use by consumers is not use by care providers, so this does not count towards level 2 or 3. Cited from the assistant's memory; not searched. To be checked by the owner before use.

source: FDA clearance of Moon Surgical ScoPilot, 2025 (via MassDevice); review in npj Digital Medicine, 2024
comment: An AI function that positions the camera during keyhole surgery was cleared in the US in March 2025; the surgeon keeps control of the instruments. A 2024 review of cleared surgical robots found 86% at the lowest level of autonomy and only two with machine-learning capabilities recognised by the regulator. Found by web search; pages not opened.

source: US ASTP data brief on the AHA IT supplement survey, 2024 (via AHA)
comment: About 71% of US hospitals reported predictive AI integrated into their electronic health record in 2024, up from 66% in 2023; 86% of hospitals in systems against 37% of independent ones. Most common uses are forecasting inpatient trajectories and flagging high-risk outpatients; use for treatment recommendations stayed low. US hospitals only. Found by web search; pages not opened.

source: Harvard Gazette on Mass General Brigham, 2025; Kaiser Permanente figures (via News-Medical)
comment: AI note-taking during patient visits is in routine use at named providers: more than 3,000 providers at Mass General Brigham by April 2025, and 7,260 physicians at Kaiser Permanente across more than 2.5 million visits between October 2023 and December 2024. No survey of actual use reaching 25% was found; one estimate says about a third of providers have access, which is not use. This is documentation support, one use of language models among several.
